tier_reason: borisbat/dasProfile README tables compare the DAS interpreter with Lua 5.5.1 and QuickJS 2026-06-04 on 16 kernels; benchmark code is public (main.das, tests/, hosts/, CMakeLists.txt pinning Lua and QuickJS tarballs by SHA256), toolchain (Clang 19.1.7 / AppleClang 21), Release build type and CPU models (Ryzen 7 PRO 8700GE, Apple M1 Max) are stated. Every quoted number matches the Linux and macOS interpreted tables.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Clang 19.1.7 on Linux, AppleClang 21.0.0.21000101 on macOS; daslang 0.6.4 SDK (consumed through find_package(DAS), built separately from the daScript repo), LLVM 22.1.5. dasProfile's CMakeLists.txt forces CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG on Clang; the '-O3' comment in the file refers to the C++ lane). Lua 5.5.1 is compiled from the SHA256-pinned lua.org tarball inside the same Release project (linit.c patched to add a profile_native module); QuickJS 2026-06-04 is built from the pinned bellard.org tarball with its upstream Makefile (hosts/quickjs_host.mk includes it), so QuickJS uses its own default flags.
corrections.caveats: The benchmark repo is written and maintained by the daslang lead developer (borisbat also merges on the daScript repo), so this is a first-party suite although it is fully public and reproducible; dasProfile shows no licence (no LICENSE file; the language repo is BSD-3-Clause). The daslang SDK's own build flags are set by the daScript repo, not stated in dasProfile. LuaJIT -joff beats the DAS interpreter on 'tree' and 'fibonacci recursive' on Linux, Mono --interpreter beats it on 'tree' on both platforms, and Lua is within about 1% on Linux fibonacci recursive (0.048174s vs 0.048747s); the Linux DAS dictionary cell has ±25% spread. A separate third-party suite (sashi0034/script-language-benchmark, Windows, Visual Studio 17 2022, code generated with Codex and flagged by its author as unreviewed, CPU not stated) reports Daslang fastest on 13 of 16 workloads against Lua and AngelScript (fibonacci_recursive 266.421 vs Lua 599.702) but Lua wins sort (6.175 vs 237.142 ms) and string2float (68.624 vs 107.174 ms); the two suites use different kernel code, so the sort result is not directly comparable with the dasProfile row where DAS wins.

notes: Numbers, ratios (27.3x vs Lua and 8.5x vs QuickJS on Linux sha256, derived from page data) and the 'all 16 kernels vs Lua and QuickJS' claim check out on the Linux table. Shortcoming: first-party suite by the daslang developer, no licence on dasProfile, DAS SDK flags not in the benchmark repo; LuaJIT -joff and Mono --interpreter beat the DAS interpreter on some kernels.

tier_reason: Independent third-party suite (ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark, v8-v7 benchmarks run by .github/workflows/update.yml on GitHub Actions) lists ant 2186/3589/2001 vs QuickJS 1217/1761/1067 vs Duktape 489/905/371 (ubuntu/macos-arm64/windows) in the 10/5/2026 snapshot. Engines come prebuilt via the ahaoboy/js-engine-setup action, no compiler flags or CPU model, so not A.

corrections.hardware: GitHub Actions hosted runners (ubuntu-latest, macos-latest arm64, windows-latest); CPU model not stated
corrections.caveats: Engines are installed as prebuilt binaries through the suite owner's ahaoboy/js-engine-setup action (strip: true) and *-build repos; compiler flags and CPU model are not stated (GitHub Actions runners), and the suite is small (59 stars), so this is third-party but short of tier A. Ant Silver has a JIT (a fork of the MIR backend) while QuickJS and Duktape are pure interpreters, so the comparison is JIT engine vs interpreters. The score is one v8-v7 aggregate (an older, partly micro-benchmark suite) and ant does not win every component: on ubuntu QuickJS beats it on RayTrace (1594 vs 1059) and Splay (3183 vs 2483). Engines are run as shells, so startup and runtime wrappers can matter. The project's own README compares only cold start and size against Node, Bun and Deno (Hono import benchmark) and does not mention QuickJS or Duktape, so the QuickJS/Duktape comparison rests only on the third-party suite. Primarily a CLI runtime; the repo has public headers (include/ant.h, isolate.h, runtime.h) that suggest an embedding API, but embedding use was not confirmed. test262 pass rate is about 66% per its README.

notes: All quoted scores and versions (ant 15.1.4977edb5.0, QuickJS 2026.06.04, Duktape 2.99.99 / 2.7.0) match the README bench tables; 1.8x QuickJS and 4.5x Duktape on ubuntu are derived from page data. Shortcoming: JIT engine compared with interpreters, prebuilt binaries on unnamed CI hardware, ant loses RayTrace and Splay to QuickJS, embedding API unconfirmed.

tier_reason: Independent third-party suite r-lyeh-archived/scriptorium (public-domain run.bat, bench.cc, tests/fib.c, c/c4jit/make.bat) ranks c4-jit 4th at 0.136 s vs Lua 1.341 s ('x09.8'). Compiler (VS2015 RC/VS2013) and c4jit flags (/Ox /Oy /MT /DNDEBUG) are public, but the CPU is given only as 'AMD A10 3.8 GHz' and the Lua binary's version and flags are not stated, so not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2015 RC where possible, Visual Studio 2013 elsewhere (README); c4jit built with 'cl /Fec4jit.exe c4x86.c /Ox /Oy /MT /DNDEBUG' (c/c4jit/make.bat); the Lua baseline is invoked as 'lua' from PATH with its version and build flags not stated (the repo vendors lua/lua-5.3.1 sources).
corrections.workload: Recursive Fibonacci fib(34) (tests/fib.c for c4-jit, tests/fib.lua for Lua; the sources' comment says 'Should return 433494437', which is fib(43), while fib(34) is 5702887), each engine launched as a standalone executable through system() by bench.cc ('bench 5'): the wall time of five whole-process runs is averaged, so process start, parsing and JIT compilation are included; the board keeps the minimum of repeated recordings in bench.csv and gives a score relative to Lua. The c4-jit row compiles the C fib to x86 machine code with c4x86.
corrections.caveats: Single micro-benchmark (recursive fib(34)); numbers are from July 2015 on a Windows 7 'AMD A10 3.8 GHz' (exact model not stated) with MSVC 2013/2015, so engine versions are very old; the page says 'take it with a grain of salt'; the Lua row is labelled LuaDist lua and run from PATH with version and build flags not stated; each time is the mean of five whole-process launches (startup and compile included), with no variance reported. The benchmark repo (scriptorium) is archived; EarlGray/c4 itself is not archived but has had no commits since 2015-07-26, and its last commit merges an 'MSVC support' patch from r-lyeh, the scriptorium author. c4x86 is 32-bit x86 only and not self-hosted per its README; the fork gives no benchmarks itself and the 9.9x figure comes only from the scriptorium fib test; toy-grade, included mainly for study.

notes: c4-jit 0.136 s vs Lua 1.341 s, rank 4 of 50, plain c4 2.538 s all match the scriptorium README; about 9.9x is derived from page data. Shortcoming: one fib micro-benchmark from 2015, Lua build unstated, whole-process timing, 32-bit x86 only, abandoned since 2015; GPL-2.0, 973 stars, fork of rswier/c4 confirmed.
